item.title: [53★] Proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis Conjecture: An Exposition
item.author: Guy Blanc, ..., Carmen Strassle, Li-Yang Tan
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 53 ★

Authors: Guy Blanc, ..., Carmen Strassle, Li-Yang Tan

arXiv ID: 2611.11626 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

We give an exposition of a recent proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, which states that every degree-dd polynomial p:{0,1}n→[0,1]p : \{0,1\}^n \to [0,1] has a variable of influence at least poly(Var(p)/d)\mathrm{poly}(\mathrm{Var}(p)/d). This implies that quantum query algorithms for decision problems can be efficiently simulated classically on most inputs. It also yields a near-equivalence between the status of the BPP\mathsf{BPP} vs. BQP\mathsf{BQP} problem in the random oracle and unrelativized worlds. We organize the proof around four main steps and discuss how each connects to the literature on the analysis of boolean functions and probabilistic combinatorics. To bring out the key ideas, we do not optimize parameters, and our presentation yields weaker exponents than the original. The proof was then shared with the authors, who worked to understand it and prepare this exposition. Anthropic's public models were used in this process. item.title: [39★] An efficient classical algorithm for OTOCs in chaotic quantum dynamics
item.author: Yunchao Liu, ..., Shreya Vardhan, Tianci Zhou
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 39 ★

Authors: Yunchao Liu, ..., Shreya Vardhan, Tianci Zhou

arXiv ID: 2611.12773 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Estimating out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs) in individual instances of random quantum circuits has been proposed as a candidate for verifiable quantum advantage, and demonstrated to be hard for conventional classical algorithms such as tensor networks and Monte Carlo. Using insights from quantum chaos, we develop and implement a polynomial-time classical algorithm for the four-point OTOC(1){\rm OTOC}^{(1)} and the eight-point OTOC(2){\rm OTOC}^{(2)} in typical instances of one-dimensional (1D) quantum circuits. Our results demonstrate average-case classical tractability of estimating OTOCs in the sensitive regime where circuit-to-circuit fluctuations are large. Our algorithm organizes the OTOC into a rapidly converging series, where the leading term includes contributions from histories within permutation degrees of freedom in the replicated Hilbert space, and subleading terms arise from excursions outside this space. Although chaos is often viewed as an insurmountable barrier to classical simulation, our algorithm exploits a form of dephasing caused by chaos, which suppresses the subleading terms. We provide strong theoretical and numerical evidence to support this suppression. Further, we demonstrate that practical implementations of our algorithm estimate OTOC(1){\rm OTOC}^{(1)} and OTOC(2){\rm OTOC}^{(2)} in 1D circuits with high accuracy, achieving higher signal-to-noise ratio at larger circuit depths compared to recent 2D experiments by Google. Extending our algorithm to higher dimensions, and resolving the status of quantum advantage in 2D OTOCs, remain open problems.

Yunchao Liu, ..., Shreya Vardhan, Tianci Zhou

item.title: [33★] Simulating the quantum switch with quantum circuits is impossible
item.author: Caisheng Cheng
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 33 ★

Authors: Caisheng Cheng

arXiv ID: 2611.10615 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

The quantum switch is a higher-order transformation that combines input quantum channels in an indefinite causal order. Whether quantum circuits can simulate its action, and how many calls to the input channels such a simulation requires, are natural questions about the power of quantum control of causal order. In this work, we prove that no quantum circuit with classically controlled causal order can exactly and deterministically simulate the quantum switch for arbitrary input channels using any finite number of calls. This impossibility holds already for qubit channels and extends to the complete rr-switch, which coherently controls all permutations of rr input channels. These results settle the question of exact deterministic circuit simulation of the quantum switch. They demonstrate that processes with indefinite causal order cannot, in general, be efficiently simulated in this setting even by quantum circuits with classically controlled causal order.

Caisheng Cheng

item.title: [31★] A short proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis Conjecture via the completion framework
item.author: Thomas Huffstutler, David Miloschewsky, Supartha Podder

Authors: Thomas Huffstutler, David Miloschewsky, Supartha Podder

arXiv ID: 2611.12795 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

We give a short proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture. If a partial Boolean function ff is defined on a δ\delta-fraction of all nn-bit strings and have quantum query complexity Q(f)Q(f), then, for every 0<ϵ<10<\epsilon<1, a deterministic algorithm computes ff correctly on at least a 1−ϵ1-\epsilon fraction of its domain using O(Q(f)6/(ϵδ)2)O( Q(f)^6 / (\epsilon \delta)^2) queries. Our proof uses the completion framework and establishes a more general bound in terms of the classical adversary measure. The only result we use from Turturean's recent proof is a special case of his certificate inequality, for which we provide a self-contained proof. We also derive the stronger variant of the Aaronson-Ambainis Conjecture, the bounded-polynomial influence conjecture, from our main result in the appendix.

item.title: [29★] A Universal Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing Architecture with Globally Driven Atom Arrays
item.author: Zhihao Zhang, ..., Lei Feng, Xiaopeng Li
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 29 ★

Authors: Zhihao Zhang, ..., Lei Feng, Xiaopeng Li

arXiv ID: 2611.12098 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Scalable quantum computation requires reconciling programmability with simple, high-fidelity control. Here, we propose a universal fault-tolerant architecture using globally driven dual-species atom arrays. In a hybrid neutral-atom system, interspecies Rydberg interactions enable qubit addressability without locally addressed quantum gates. We construct a universal native instruction set, Global Rydberg Atom Instruction Language (GRAIL), and show that crosstalk errors can be suppressed to the 10−410^{-4} level. We compile surface-code error correction and magic state cultivation into GRAIL, and parallelize the compilation to suppress crosstalk. Under a hardware-inferred circuit-level noise model, we obtain an error-correction threshold of 1.43%1.43\% for the resulting quantum memory and a logical error rate below 10−910^{-9} for magic states cultivated at an experimentally accessible Rydberg Rabi frequency. By replacing local gate addressing with atom-mediated selectivity, this architecture removes the associated calibration requirements, offering a route to simpler control for large-scale fault-tolerant neutral-atom computation.

item.title: [25★] Regev's Reduction Reaches Reconstruction
item.author: Stephen P. Jordan, Quynh T. Nguyen, Leo Zhou
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 25 ★

Authors: Stephen P. Jordan, Quynh T. Nguyen, Leo Zhou

arXiv ID: 2611.10283 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Regev's reduction uses a quantum Fourier transform to carry out reductions between various problems related to lattices and codes. We apply it to the problem of sampling from Gibbs distributions of certain classical spin glass Hamiltonians, which can equivalently be thought of as cost functions for average-case instances of an optimization problem called DD-regular max-kk-LINSAT. This problem becomes hard at low temperature. Here, we use a quantum decoding algorithm called Belief Propagation with Quantum Messages (BPQM) to solve the decoding problem arising from Regev's reduction. Our main contribution is a proof that the minimum temperature reachable using Regev+BPQM is exactly equal to the reconstruction threshold temperature for noisy channels transmitting signals on a tree network. This equality can be understood via Renes' duality between classical and quantum channels, which we use to show that quantum decoding is possible exactly when classical reconstruction on the dual problem is impossible. Mézard and Montanari identified this reconstruction temperature with a dynamical glass transition predicted by the one-step replica-symmetry breaking (1RSB) cavity equation. It is conjectured that local samplers such as Metropolis Monte Carlo and Glauber dynamics cannot equilibrate efficiently below this reconstruction temperature but may do so above it; our large numerical experiments show close agreement with this prediction across hundreds of different problem parameters. Therefore, our results rigorously show that Regev+BPQM reaches a temperature for which, to our knowledge, there is no matching classical guarantee, and brings Regev+BPQM to the conjectured limit of efficient Gibbs sampling by classical local dynamics.

Stephen P. Jordan, Quynh T. Nguyen, Leo Zhou

item.title: [24★] No Exponential Quantum Advantage for Decoded Quantum Interferometry with Local Quantum Decoders
item.author: Brandon Augustino, ..., Shreehari Sureshbabu, Jacob Watkins
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 24 ★

Authors: Brandon Augustino, ..., Shreehari Sureshbabu, Jacob Watkins

arXiv ID: 2611.12718 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) reduces optimization of sparse linear constraint problems, and sampling from their Gibbs measures, to decoding a linear code from a quantum state. We study DQI on random DD-regular kk-sparse instances with k≥3k\ge3, for which local decoders such as belief propagation with quantum messages (BPQM) are commonly used. Such decoders estimate a typical codeword symbol using only the qudits within logarithmic distance of it. Our main insight is that the thresholds of the decoding problem induced by DQI correspond to phase transitions of the Gibbs measure that are well studied in statistical physics: tree reconstruction for local decoders and, for Max-kk-XORSAT, condensation for the optimal decoder. This insight allows us to prove two main results. First, we prove an information-theoretic obstruction: no local decoder can recover the codeword with high probability above the tree reconstruction threshold. Conversely, we show that a decoder based on BPQM reaches this threshold. Since the cavity method predicts that local Markov chains equilibrate rapidly up to the same threshold, we expect DQI with local decoders to give no exponential speedup for sampling and no advantage in approximate optimization with amplitude functions that depend only on the number of violated constraints. Second, we consider the optimal decoder (the pretty-good measurement, for which no efficient implementation is known) and show that it succeeds exactly below the condensation threshold. The condensation threshold thus provides a tight upper bound on the performance of DQI with these amplitude functions, providing a strict refinement of the limit that Jordan et al.\ derived from the Holevo bound. Our results point to efficient nonlocal decoders that succeed between the two thresholds as the only viable path to a quantum advantage with DQI on these instances.

Brandon Augustino, ..., Shreehari Sureshbabu, Jacob Watkins

item.title: [24★] Efficient classical simulation of Fermi-Hubbard models with Kramers symmetry
item.author: Chaithanya Rayudu, ..., Ojas Parekh, Andrew Zhao
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 24 ★

Authors: Chaithanya Rayudu, ..., Ojas Parekh, Andrew Zhao

arXiv ID: 2611.10039 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Quantum Monte Carlo methods are widely used to solve quantum many-body problems. However, rigorous guarantees for their performance are poorly understood, especially for simulating interacting fermions. In this work, we develop a quantum Monte Carlo algorithm for a broad family of fermionic systems exhibiting Kramers time-reversal symmetry, and prove that their partition functions can be estimated in polynomial time. This family, which contains many important classes of Hubbard-type models, is known to both avoid the sign problem and obey a Lee-Yang zero-freeness theorem. Thus our results suggest that these two properties together may enable efficient classical algorithms for quantum many-body systems more broadly.

Chaithanya Rayudu, ..., Ojas Parekh, Andrew Zhao

item.title: [17★] GARI++: A General-Purpose Decoder for Quantum Error Correction
item.author: Arshpreet Singh Maan, ..., Valentin Savin, Alexandru Paler
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 17 ★

Authors: Arshpreet Singh Maan, ..., Valentin Savin, Alexandru Paler

arXiv ID: 2611.12833 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

We present GARI++, a two-stage decoding pipeline achieving accuracy competitive with the state of the art across surface, bivariate bicycle and color codes without relying on ensembles. The first stage uses GARI, a normalized min-sum decoder with random serial scheduling on the GARI transformed matrix. The second stage decoder is used only for the cases that the first stage does not converge, and the decoder is configurable based on the choice of the QEC code. The first stage pipelines towards the second stage both the residual syndrome and the soft information. GARI++ pipelining is predictive, meaning that GARI++ chooses the first stage iteration outputs which are expected to deliver the best accuracy in the second stage. GARI++ motivates a hybrid FPGA-CPU architecture for real-time decoding. For example, under uniform circuit-level depolarising noise with a physical error rate of 0.001, the FPGA implementation of GARI achieves average latencies per round ranging from 201ns201 ns to 11.8μs11.8\mu s for surface code distances between 7 and 25. At the same time, due to the very low weight residuals output by the first stage, the average residual decoding time per round remains near constant and below one microsecond on a single Apple M2 core for surface code distances even up to 51 when using Union-Find and accuracy on par with correlated MWPM.

Arshpreet Singh Maan, ..., Valentin Savin, Alexandru Paler

item.title: [16★] Commuting-check gauging for fault-tolerant logical measurements
item.author: Zongyuan Wang
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 16 ★

Authors: Zongyuan Wang

arXiv ID: 2611.12236 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Gauging turns a logical operator into a product of local checks, providing a route to logical measurement and lattice surgery. These checks can fail to commute outside the code space, so measuring one can randomize the outcome of another. In this work, we introduce completion qubits that make the checks commute for Clifford Z2\mathbb{Z}_2 symmetries of qubit stabilizer codes. Adding one completion qubit per noncommuting pair preserves the gauged code space and its distance while keeping the checks Clifford. Completion also preserves the low-density parity-check property with a constant-factor qubit overhead. We generalize completion to qudits and establish bounds on the Clifford-hierarchy level of the completed checks in prime dimensions. Global commutation ensures that a fault-free round fixes the syndrome until the next fault and allows us to bound fault propagation independently of the number of measurement rounds. For qubit codes, we show that gauging and ungauging a distance-dd parent code implements a logical measurement with circuit fault distance Ω(d)\Omega(d) in O(d)O(d) rounds. We demonstrate the construction by gauging two toric codes into the D(D4)D(D_4) quantum double and back, with an explicit circuit whose circuit fault distance equals the parent code distance. Our results provide a framework for fault-tolerant logical measurements using commuting checks, with applications to magic-state preparation by lattice surgery.

Zongyuan Wang

item.title: [10★] Bridging Gaps with Tensor Networks: From the Haldane Gap and Beyond
item.author: Sirui Lu
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 10 ★

Authors: Sirui Lu

arXiv ID: 2611.11049 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Proofs generated by large language models are often difficult to understand, generalize, or formalize directly. Here we verify, digest, and formalize OpenAI's computer-assisted proof of a uniform gap in the periodic spin-1 Heisenberg chain using tensor-network diagrams and Lean 4. Reading the partition-function network along space and imaginary time shows how finite-ring bounds propagate across doubled lengths and inverse temperatures to all longer even rings, sharpening the spin-1 bound from the same finite inputs by a factor of 19 to ΔL>0.0729\Delta_L > 0.0729 for all even L≥36L \geq 36. We identify reflection positivity as the general condition behind the proof and certify uniform gaps in seven additional spin chains and ladders. More broadly, digesting machine-generated proofs into transparent physical mechanisms yields sharper bounds, broader theorems, and reusable formal verifications.

Sirui Lu

Abstract:

We construct a recursive oracle OO and a unary language L∈EQPO∖(IPO∪PHO)L\in\mathsf{EQP}^O\setminus(\mathsf{IP}^O\cup\mathsf{PH}^O), strengthening the BQP\mathsf{BQP} versus IP\mathsf{IP} oracle separation of Bouland et al. to exact quantum computation. item.title: [6★] Pauli propagation in adaptive local frames
item.author: Jonnathan Pineda-Jiménez, Mario Collura
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 6 ★

Authors: Jonnathan Pineda-Jiménez, Mario Collura

arXiv ID: 2611.11647 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

The cost of Pauli propagation depends on the local basis in which the evolving operator is expanded. We show that its Pauli complexity splits into an occupation part, invariant under local rotations and bounded from below by the operator mass and length distributions, and a flavour part that a suitable basis can remove. We introduce frame-adaptive Pauli propagation (FAPP), which rotates the basis of every qubit, gate by gate, to the principal axes of the operator's local polarisation, exactly and within the memory structure of Pauli propagation. This simple rule achieves most of what the best local frame can, and the polarisation predicts how much any local frame can gain. In the Ising chain in transverse and longitudinal fields, FAPP lowers the truncation error at fixed memory by up to an order of magnitude and the memory by a size-independent factor of three; on the infinite two-dimensional lattice it needs up to seven times fewer strings for a given certified accuracy, and in Clifford circuits doped with T gates two to eight times fewer.

Jonnathan Pineda-Jiménez, Mario Collura

item.title: [5★] Testing non-classical gravitational phase dynamics under strong dephasing
item.author: Tianfeng Feng, Vlatko Vedral
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 5 ★

Authors: Tianfeng Feng, Vlatko Vedral

arXiv ID: 2611.12229 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Whether gravity must be quantum is often approached by asking whether two masses can become entangled through their mutual gravitational interaction. In practice, the weak interaction competes with environmental decoherence, so the final state may contain no entanglement even when the underlying gravitational phase remains coherent. We investigate what can still be learned from the dynamics in a dephased Bose--Marletto--Vedral setup. The dominant Newtonian effect for well-separated paths is an accumulated phase rather than transfer between interferometer arms, a regime motivated by matter-wave gravitational phase experiments and quantified here by wavepacket-overlap and deflection estimates. Keeping independently characterized local which-path dephasing fixed, we prove an exact finite-time distinction between the gravitational conditional-phase evolution and every passive stochastic local-phase model (induced by a classical mediator), including regimes where the chosen input remains separable at all times. The distinction survives, with a modified sensitivity, when the comparison is enlarged to population-preserving classical measurement and feedback through a diagonal PPT relaxation. These results identify an operational test of gravitational phase dynamics in the strong-dephasing regimes, conditional on explicit and physically motivated classical mediator models.

Tianfeng Feng, Vlatko Vedral

item.title: [4★] Unbounded advantage of adaptivity in entanglement-assisted communication
item.author: Armin Tavakoli
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 4 ★

Authors: Armin Tavakoli

arXiv ID: 2611.11333 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Shared entanglement can reduce the amount of classical communication needed to perform distributed computation. This can be achieved either by first measuring the entanglement and then communicating classically, or by adapting the quantum measurement to the received message. Here, we introduce tasks that adaptive protocols can solve using just three entanglement-assisted messages, while the communication cost grows without bound when the quantum receiver is not adaptive. Consequently, no bounded amount of classical communication can reproduce all correlations generated by an entanglement-assisted ternary classical channel. We establish two complementary limitations on the relation between adaptive and non-adaptive quantum protocols. First, every adaptive protocol using a finite entanglement dimension admits a non-adaptive simulation at finite communication cost. Second, every adaptive protocol sending dd messages can be simulated to within error ε\varepsilon using O(dlog(1/ε))O(d\log(1/\varepsilon)) non-adaptive messages. Our results reveal the fundamentally unbounded advantage of adaptivity in quantum communication, but also that observing very large advantages requires both high-dimensional entanglement and very precise observations.

Armin Tavakoli

item.title: [4★] BP-based qLDPC Decoding under Long-range Correlated Noise: Trapping Configurations and Prior Mismatch
item.author: Abhinav Dangi, Avhishek Chatterjee
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 4 ★

Authors: Abhinav Dangi, Avhishek Chatterjee

arXiv ID: 2611.10796 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

We study the robustness of two state-of-the-art BP-based qLDPC decoders, Relay-BP and beam search, designed for independent noise when applied to spatially correlated noise with unchanged single-mechanism error probabilities. We generate correlated errors with a hidden Gaussian Markov random field, which lets us control the strength and range of the correlation while keeping every marginal error probability exact. This setting complements correlation-aware decoding: it asks how existing decoders perform when their assumed joint error model is mismatched. Across multiple tested circuits and code instances that we simulated, we observe that correlations can change logical error rates by orders of magnitude, reduce the finite-size distance advantage, and alter the relative ranking of Relay-BP, beam search, and BP-OSD. On one of the two tested circuits, Relay-BP and beam search become worse than BP-OSD, and increasing relay memory or beam width does not compensate for the degradation. Configuration analysis indicates that correlation primarily increases the probability of trapping configurations that are known to challenge these decoders; at matched error weight, correlated errors still cause decoding failures several times more often than i.i.d. errors. Finally, supplying the decoders with the marginals conditioned on the hidden field recovers most of the lost performance in the tested settings identifying prior mismatch as a major contributor to performance degradation under correlation.

Abhinav Dangi, Avhishek Chatterjee

item.title: [3★] Lieb-Robinson bound for one-dimensional continuum fermions
item.author: Marius Lemm, Hailun Lu, Harman Preet Singh
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 3 ★

Authors: Marius Lemm, Hailun Lu, Harman Preet Singh

arXiv ID: 2611.11655 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

The central difficulty in quantum many-body physics is that the Hilbert space dimension grows exponentially with the total degrees of freedom. A key feature to circumvent this problem is locality, which manifests dynamically through an approximate causal structure in the form of a Lieb-Robinson bound (LRB). LRBs have been proved for quantum spin systems and certain lattice boson systems, but so far never for realistic continuum systems. We present the first LRB that applies to a standard system of one-dimensional continuum fermions. It applies to initial states with controlled moments of local particle number and energy and is thus thermodynamically stable. Our result breaks the main technical barrier that has existed for using the vast locality toolbox on continuum systems.

Marius Lemm, Hailun Lu, Harman Preet Singh

item.title: [3★] Quantum entanglement as a resource for self-organization and stabilization
item.author: Kazuki Ikeda
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 3 ★

Authors: Kazuki Ikeda

arXiv ID: 2611.11175 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Can quantum entanglement generate macroscopic order that persists after the entanglement itself disappears? We establish such a mechanism in a driven-dissipative bosonic lattice, where local entanglement enables transport that amplifies spatial fluctuations into extended Turing patterns. For the full nonlinear dynamics with noise and disorder, we derive rigorous finite-time bounds on pattern intensity for all admissible separable evolutions, allowing arbitrary classical correlations. Quantum dynamics produces pattern intensities beyond these bounds during both formation and stabilization under noise. The excess intensity also provides a lower bound on the accumulated transport contribution beyond the separable limit. We further introduce an environment that responds to emerging order by suppressing local coherence and activating classical transport. The patterns then persist as local entanglement is lost, with both stages arising from a single time-independent Lindblad equation. These results show how transient quantum resources can establish persistent macroscopic order, opening new directions for harnessing self-organization in nonequilibrium systems.

Kazuki Ikeda

item.title: [3★] Markov-Shielded Typicality for Thermal Quantum States
item.author: Atsushi Iwaki, Chisa Hotta
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 3 ★

Authors: Atsushi Iwaki, Chisa Hotta

arXiv ID: 2611.10593 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Pure states of quantum many-body systems at thermal equilibrium are known to be typical, in a sense that a randomly chosen pure state from an appropriate energy shell reproduces the Gibbs-state expectation values of most observables acting on a small subsystem. However, such typical states are intrinsically stochastic, conventionally generated from the random high-temperature state, suffer from statistical fluctuations, and do not provide a continuous connection to the ground state. Here, we introduce a deterministic variational framework for constructing a Markov-Shielded Typical (MST) state, a unique thermal pure-state representative whose local reduced density matrices closely approximate those of the Gibbs state, from the ground state up to infinite-temperature limit. Our approach reformulates free-energy minimization by replacing the nonlocal von Neumann entropy with a local, computationally tractable Markov entropy, where we establish rigorous upper and lower bounds of MST free energy to lie in the very vicinity of the thermal free energy. This framework extends the concept of typicality to deterministic pure-state representations of thermal equilibrium, offering a scalable wave-function approach with potential applications to both classical and quantum computing.

Atsushi Iwaki, Chisa Hotta

item.title: [2★] The simulability frontiers of photonic quantum computing
item.author: Jean Senellart, ..., Shane Mansfield, Pierre-Emmanuel Emeriau
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 2 ★

Authors: Jean Senellart, ..., Shane Mansfield, Pierre-Emmanuel Emeriau

arXiv ID: 2611.12876 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Estimates of when photonic devices outgrow classical simulation are hard to compare: even for single-photon boson sampling, quoted thresholds range from 50 to 98 photons, as they rest on different tasks and assumptions. We propose as a common unit the time a classical computer needs to draw one sample from the device's exact output distribution, up to floating-point rounding. Only exactness applies equally to every kind of light, since the cost of approximate sampling depends on the accuracy required. The simulability frontier is the device size at which our fastest exact sampler produces one sample per second on a fixed machine; this device size increases with better hardware and algorithms. As the time per sample grows exponentially with the number of detected photons, doubling the machine speed moves the frontier by about one photon, whereas a better algorithm changes the growth rate. We measure the frontier with photonic-engines, an open-source GPU library of exact samplers for single photons, entangled photons from quantum emitters, vacuum-single-photon superpositions and squeezed light. Each sampler is validated against a simulator sharing no code with it. On one NVIDIA H100 GPU, with Haar-random interferometers, twice as many modes as photonic inputs and photon-number-resolving detectors, the frontier lies at 38.3 single photons and at 31.0 entangled photons from one emitter. For squeezed light, a timing model fitted to measurements places it at 41.5 squeezed photonic inputs of mean photon number 0.5. For our samplers, coherence alone makes simulation harder: sources that emit a photon with probability one half reach 64.2 when vacuum and photon are mixed incoherently, as for lossy single photons, but only 50.0 when they are in coherent superposition. Feed-forward from mid-circuit measurement of up to three modes lowers the single-photon frontier only from 38.3 to 38.1.

Jean Senellart, ..., Shane Mansfield, Pierre-Emmanuel Emeriau

item.title: [2★] Reducing Provers in Distributed Quantum Verification
item.author: Alex Della Schiava, ..., François Le Gall, Harumichi Nishimura
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 2 ★

Authors: Alex Della Schiava, ..., François Le Gall, Harumichi Nishimura

arXiv ID: 2611.12600 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

In the distributed quantum Merlin-Arthur (dQMA\mathsf{dQMA}) model introduced by Fraigniaud, Le Gall, Nishimura, and Paz (ITCS 2021), a network of quantum computers verifies a global property with the aid of a quantum proof supplied by an untrusted prover. While the nodes are computationally unbounded, the challenge is to limit proof size and the communication required for verification. In this paper, we consider the model of Hasegawa, Kundu, and Nishimura (PODC 2024), where the proof must be unentangled across nodes, and define its extension to kk unentangled provers, denoted by dQMAS(k)\mathsf{dQMAS}(k). In this setting, we investigate the proof size per node and the communication costs of reducing the number of provers. Our first result reduces the number of provers from kk to two, doubling the proof size without additional communication. Moreover, with four additional rounds, we can reduce the number of provers from kk to one, using at most three times the original local proof size plus a logarithmic term in the number of nodes. Finally, we establish amplification for perfectly complete protocols. In this regime, a single prover suffices with a constant-factor overhead in our reductions, yielding dQMAS=dQMAS(k)\mathsf{dQMAS} = \mathsf{dQMAS}(k).

Alex Della Schiava, ..., François Le Gall, Harumichi Nishimura

item.title: [2★] All-to-all connectivity via adiabatic ZZ interactions in a superconducting flux qubit processor
item.author: Elena Lupo, ..., Eran Ginossar, Michael Stern
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 2 ★

Authors: Elena Lupo, ..., Eran Ginossar, Michael Stern

arXiv ID: 2611.12576 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Scalable superconducting quantum processors would benefit from high qubit connectivity, yet existing architectures connect neighbouring qubits via tunable couplers, which introduce substantial wiring and control overhead. Here, we propose a baseband-driven adiabatic ZZ gate that entangles any selected pair in a register of flux qubits coupled via a common cavity. The qubits stay dc-biased at their flux sweet spot. Strong drives applied selectively through local flux lines, at frequencies far below the qubit transitions, adiabatically tilt the quantization axes and generate an effective longitudinal ZZ interaction. The strength of the coupling is tunable and controlled by the amplitudes and relative phase of the drives rather than by any resonance condition. Numerical simulations give coherent gate errors below 10−410^{-4} over broad ranges of drive frequency, with comparable fidelities for two simultaneous gates in a four-qubit register. The protocol is robust against frequency fluctuations and remains effective even when many qubits are coupled to the cavity.

Authors: Luis Adrián Lizama-Pérez, José Mauricio López-Romero

arXiv ID: 2611.11754 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

We investigate advantage distillation for paired-state Loop-Back quantum key distribution, with a fixed optical station serving a lightweight portable terminal. Alice prepares two polarization-encoded pulses, Bob selects and applies a polarization filter to each pulse, and Alice infers his selections from the returned detection pattern. The proposed advantage-distillation step selects consistent blocks of three two-bit records using two independent public parity checks on a minimal connected graph. The closing edge of a parity polygon is shown to be redundant: any spanning tree of the same vertices has the same acceptance set. We derive exact acceptance probabilities, residual-error laws, and retention rates. Under independent bit errors, the three-record filter reduces the leading error term from e to e^2, while its cost in discarded records and public information is accounted for explicitly. A modular security theorem bounds the additional guessing advantage available to an adversary after syndrome disclosure and block acceptance, including arbitrary quantum side information. We also evaluate a specified single-photon passive-tap optical channel, obtaining a positive conditional entropy bound and exact accepted-block security quantities. This parity-based advantage-distillation step detects discrepancies by postselection; it does not correct individual errors and is intended to precede conventional reconciliation. The architecture suggests two further directions: hybrid filtering and reconciliation, and key establishment between portable users accessing a shared quantum station.

item.content:encoded:
Scites: 2 ★

Authors: Ankit Khandelwal, ..., Dhinakaran Vinayagamurthy, M Girish Chandra

arXiv ID: 2611.11084 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) requires the calculation of highly accurate electronic-structure energies and nuclear forces at every time step, which can quickly become computationally expensive. Sample-based quantum diagonalization offers a route to such calculations on quantum hardware, but its use in AIMD simulations has so far been limited to active spaces of about 20 qubits. In these spaces, exact diagonalization is tractable, and the quantum circuits are typically built from standard coupled-cluster amplitudes. Here, we introduce SqDRIFT-AIMD, which combines randomized sample-based Krylov quantum diagonalization (SqDRIFT) with analytical nuclear gradients. With SqDRIFT-AIMD, we obtain more accurate ground-state energies than the conventional coupled-cluster singles and doubles (CCSD) driven AIMD simulation for the 4040-qubit active space. We apply SqDRIFT-AIMD to study the dynamics of proton transfer in the Zundel cation, using circuits executed on IBM Heron r3 quantum processors. SqDRIFT energies fall below CCSD across the 4040-qubit double-well PES and stay within a few mEhE_\text{h} of CCSD at 52 qubits. The 4040-qubit SqDRIFT-AIMD trajectory tracks the SHCI-driven proton transfer to within 1.331.33 mÅ and exhibits excellent total energy conservation, with a standard deviation of only 0.2450.245 mEhE_\text{h}. These results extend quantum-centric AIMD to active spaces beyond the reach of exact diagonalization.

item.title: [2★] Trainability-Simulability Tradeoff in Parameterized IQP-based Reinforcement Learning Policies
item.author: André Sequeira
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 2 ★

Authors: André Sequeira

arXiv ID: 2611.10793 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Parameterized instantaneous quantum polynomial-time (IQP) circuits generate distributions conjectured to be hard to sample classically. As reinforcement learning (RL) policies, their 2n2^n measurement outcomes are typically mapped to a smaller action space by a classical decoder. This aggregation can mitigate initialization concentration while making the policy classically simulable. We characterize this tradeoff through the decoder's Fourier--Pauli expansion. Under independent uniform initialization, we express policy variance as an exact sum over groups of nonconstant Pauli components with identical active-generator signatures. Each group contributes its squared aggregate coefficient times 2−r2^{-r}, where rr is the binary rank of its active generators. An inverse-polynomial aggregate coefficient with logarithmic rank prevents exponential policy concentration. Sparse Pauli expansions and contiguous action bins permit efficient classical additive estimation of action probabilities. We introduce a majority decoder combining protected low-weight components with exponentially large exact Fourier support, preserving initialization nonconcentration while excluding polynomial-size enumeration of the exact expansion. Numerical experiments corroborate the variance laws. In ten-qubit CartPole experiments, majority achieves higher returns than recursive parity and the tested local readouts, while higher-weight Pauli sectors contribute an increasing relative share of gradient magnitude during training. A complementary 21-qubit block-chain policy outperforms an extensive pool of fully connected classical neural networks in episode efficiency, even though its bounded-width structure permits efficient classical simulation. These results guide decoder design for quantum and quantum-inspired RL, distinguishing policy nonconcentration, learning performance, and classical simulability.

André Sequeira

item.title: [2★] On the estimation of linear-optical amplitudes and probabilities with entangled input state
item.author: Jean Senellart, Pierre-Emmanuel Emeriau
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 2 ★

Authors: Jean Senellart, Pierre-Emmanuel Emeriau

arXiv ID: 2611.10500 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Most proposed applications of boson samplers, including photonic machine-learning models, do not use the samples themselves but estimates of output probabilities, marginals or overlaps, obtained to additive precision from a finite number of shots. For product inputs such as single photons, these quantities can already be estimated classically with Gurvits's algorithm and its generalisations. We ask whether entangled inputs change this picture. For any nn-photon input that is a matrix-product state of bond dimension χ\chi, with one photon per site and LL modes per site, we give an unbiased estimator of any output amplitude of an mm-mode interferometer, whose mean-square error after NN draws is at most ‖ψ‖2/N\|\psi\|^2/N whatever the interferometer, the output pattern and the entanglement of the state. Each draw costs O(nLχ2+nL3+mn)O(nL\chi^2+nL^3+mn) operations after O(nLχ3)O(nL\chi^3) preprocessing, and an additive error ε\varepsilon with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta requires O(‖ψ‖2ε−2log(1/δ))O(\|\psi\|^2\varepsilon^{-2}\log(1/\delta)) draws, with memory of the order of the input size. The main application is to light emitted sequentially by quantum emitters, such as spin-based sources of photonic cluster states, for which χ\chi is bounded by the dimension of the source's retained quantum memory: one spin gives χ=2\chi=2 at any length, and a memory of kk qubits, held in emitters or in photons stored in a delay line, gives χ≤2k\chi\le2^k, so the cost stays polynomial as long as k=O(logn)k=O(\log n). The same sampler also estimates traced-memory probabilities, overlaps and individual marginal probabilities. All guarantees are additive: the estimator gives neither relative estimates of exponentially small probabilities nor a sampler of the output distribution.

Jean Senellart, Pierre-Emmanuel Emeriau

item.title: [2★] Bayes-Optimal Quantum Computational Sensing via Convex Spectral Design
item.author: Amirhossein Taherpour, Alireza Sadeghi, Georgios B. Giannakis
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 2 ★

Authors: Amirhossein Taherpour, Alireza Sadeghi, Georgios B. Giannakis

arXiv ID: 2611.10146 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Quantum computational sensing performs task-specific inference directly through coherent sensing dynamics, avoiding an intermediate estimation step. Existing designs, however, typically optimize quantum control parameters through nonconvex programs whose performance can depend strongly on initialization. This contribution formulates binary phase classification directly in terms of the sensor's measurement response. For a fixed query budget, generalized quantum signal processing (GQSP) restricts this response to a bounded trigonometric polynomial, while the Bayes classification error is linear in the response. These properties yield an exact finite-dimensional semidefinite program for the globally Bayes-optimal sensor response. Fejér--Riesz factorization and GQSP synthesis then recover a physically realizable control sequence. The same formulation extends naturally to sample-based design and additive phase uncertainty. Numerical tests show improved accuracy and optimization reliability over direct control-angle training; noise-aware redesign also lowers error under phase uncertainty.

Amirhossein Taherpour, Alireza Sadeghi, Georgios B. Giannakis

item.title: [2★] Roadmap on Nanoscale Superconductivity for Quantum Technologies

Authors: Oleksandr Dobrovolskiy, ..., Martin Gmitra, et al (44)

arXiv ID: 2611.10076 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

In 2025, the Year of Quantum Science and Technology, we celebrate a century of quantum mechanics, witnessing a surge in activities that illuminate its inherent strangeness and drive technological innovation. Superconductivity, discovered 114 years ago, stands as a prime example, offering direct and compelling evidence of macroscopic quantum phenomena. Beyond its ability to conduct immense currents without loss, superconductivity reveals the quantum realm operating on a scale we can directly observe and manipulate. The macroscopic quantum coherence, where an ensemble of particles is described by a single wave function, leads to remarkable consequences: dissipation-less current and flux quantization - the basic properties exploited in superconducting quantum circuit fabrication. This Roadmap has been inspired by intensive discussions and collaborations emerging from the European COST Action CA21144 (SuperQuMap - Superconducting Nanodevices and Quantum Materials for Coherent Manipulation). The roadmap outlines the network's concrete activities, driving advancements in superconductor-based quantum technologies and charting future directions. Spanning fundamental research to practical applications, the roadmap incorporates insights from industry partners developing quantum computation. It begins by exploring quantum materials, highlighting how topology and electronic correlations could catalyze a quantum leap in technology. We then delve into manipulating the superconducting phase, leveraging advancements in magnetism, 3D fabrication, and tunable correlations. Further, we showcase the advanced microscopy techniques - such as angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy and scanning probes - used to visualize quantum behavior. Finally, and crucially, we detail the quantum devices developed within the network, and their transformative impact on modern quantum computing approaches.

Oleksandr Dobrovolskiy, ..., Martin Gmitra, et al (44)

item.title: [1★] Dephasing-Induced Melting of Crystalline Spectral Form Factors
item.author: Preethi Gopalakrishnan, Adolfo del Campo
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 1 ★

Authors: Preethi Gopalakrishnan, Adolfo del Campo

arXiv ID: 2611.12888 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Long-range spectral order can be probed using spectral form factors, where it manifests itself as sharp Bragg peaks at integer multiples of the Heisenberg time in nearly crystalline spectra. We examine how energy dephasing in open systems affects this spectral order and how to control it. We find that Bragg peaks fade algebraically with revival order and dephasing strength, KBragg(p)∝(γp)−1/2K_{\rm Bragg}(p)\propto(\gamma p)^{-1/2}, within an extensive intermediate regime, and persist up to the lifetime of nearest-neighbor coherences despite an extreme decoherence rate. Our results establish the spectral form factor as a probe of spectral order in open quantum systems and identify temporal correlations in spectral fluctuations as a means of controlling it.

item.author: Zixiang Hong

Authors: Zixiang Hong

arXiv ID: 2611.12882 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

We develop a first-principles framework connecting microscopic waveguide scattering to quantum error correction and algorithmic performance. For polarization-encoded single photons interacting with an ensemble of two-level atoms in a chiral waveguide, we derive an effective polarization quantum channel by tracing out the frequency degree of freedom. Using this channel as the physical noise model for a rotated planar code, we observe threshold behavior as the number of atoms NN and the atom-waveguide coupling strength Γ\Gamma are varied. An asymptotic analysis of the microscopic scattering model explains the threshold scaling with NΓ/σN\Gamma/\sigma, where σ\sigma is the photon spectral bandwidth. For identical, lossless atoms with symmetric real coupling and a photon spectrum centered at resonance, the effective noise is strongly biased toward XX errors. We then incorporate the resulting logical errors into quantum phase estimation and demonstrate that the noise bias can guide circuit design. In particular, a Hadamard-basis implementation reduces sensitivity to the dominant error, improving algorithmic performance.

arXiv ID: 2611.12779 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

We propose a unified architecture for two-qubit gates in neutral-atom quantum processors which allows the implementation of the complete set of two-qubit gates. Our approach rests on a single resource that unlocks the entire gate set: an XXZ interaction with tunable anisotropy, combined only with single-qubit operations. We introduce a Rydberg-atom realization of the tunable XXZ interaction and combine it with optimally controlled global microwave pulses to implement the B, QFT, iSWAP, and √iSWAP\sqrt{\mathrm{iSWAP}} gates, as well as a continuous gate family interpolating from CZ to iSWAP via the B gate. This work allows the implementation of any two-qubit gate natively in neutral-atom platforms, enabling flexible switching between instruction sets to reduce circuit depth and compilation overhead in quantum algorithm implementation.

Authors: Amitoj S. Miglani, ..., Balsant S. Tiwari, Vishvendra S. Poonia

Abstract:

Chiral molecular bridges between silicon quantum dots can provide novel two-qubit entangling resources via the chirality-induced spin-selectivity (CISS) effect. We evaluate this using Makhlin invariants. Modeling a phase-coherent bridge as an SU(2)\mathrm{SU}(2)-valued hopping between two spins, a Schrieffer-Wolff reduction yields a twisted exchange interaction JS1⋅RS2J \mathbf{S}_1 \cdot \mathbf{R} \mathbf{S}_2, whose Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya and symmetric anisotropic parts are fixed by a single bridge angle α\alpha. Using the Kaplan-Shekhtman-Entin-Wohlman-Aharony (KSEA) gauge argument, we prove this interaction is locally equivalent to isotropic exchange; thus, a single chiral bond does not constitute a new entangling class. Breaking this gauge symmetry reveals genuine chiral utility: chiral exchange converts a uniform transverse field into a synthetic gradient, bringing the two-qubit propagator within 7×10−47\times10^{-4} of the CNOT class in invariant space 4.7 times faster than an equivalent orthogonal gradient. Shuttling a spin through bridges with non-collinear axes implements a non-Abelian SU(2)\mathrm{SU}(2) holonomy, yielding rotationally non-reciprocal transport and closed-loop geometric gates that suppress dynamical-phase noise to second order. To address the unsettled microscopic origin of CISS, we introduce a unified transport channel combining coherent rotation, a direction-reversing spin filter, and pointer-basis dephasing. This model obeys an exact tanh\tanh composition law for pumped polarization and a closed-form transverse decay law, yielding four observables that experimentally over-determine the bridge's coherent fraction FcF_c. Finally, we quantify silicon-specific hardware constraints, establishing the Landau-Zener valley-adiabaticity window (Ev≥2.1√ℏvE_v \geq 2.1\sqrt{\hbar v}) and charge-noise limit (σJ/J≤3%\sigma_J/J \leq 3\%) required for 99%99\% gate fidelity.

item.author: Bartłomiej Sikorski, Adam Sawicki
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 1 ★

Authors: Bartłomiej Sikorski, Adam Sawicki

arXiv ID: 2611.12549 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

We describe the projective orbits of complex spinors from the point of view of the momentum map. We treat the irreducible spin modules in odd dimensions 1,3,5,7,9,11 and the half-spin modules in even dimensions 2,4,6,8,10,12,14, which are the only cases with finitely many orbits. In the Clifford--Fock model, we construct representatives as sums of pure basis spinors, and the coefficients are chosen so that the representative is a critical point of the squared norm of the momentum map. The resulting momentum values in a fixed Weyl chamber distinguish the orbits. Completeness follows from Vinberg's theory of graded Lie algebras and stabilizer actions, independently of the classical spinor classifications. We recover the classical counts of 1,1,1,2,3,5 orbits in the odd cases and 1,1,1,2,2,4,9 in the even cases, and compute the projective dimension of every orbit. In dimension fourteen we also determine the closure order of the orbits, using the fact that the minimum of the squared momentum norm increases strictly under degeneration.

Abstract:

In this paper, we study the gauge dependence of quantum precision in ultrastrongly coupled light--matter systems. The unitary between gauges carries the coupling gg, so each truncation defines a different family. The quantum Fisher information traces an exact parabola across frames. Harmonic matter minimizes it at a universal θ∗=Ω/(Ω+ω)\theta_\ast=\Omega/(\Omega+\omega), set by the matter and cavity frequencies. Only the minimal-coupling bound is attainable. Frames differ by a factor 9.69.6 with opposite trends. Diverging virtual-excitation gain at the Dicke point is a gauge artifact and saturates.

item.author: Denis Stanev, Nicolò Spagnolo, Fabio Sciarrino
item.content:encoded:

Authors: Denis Stanev, Nicolò Spagnolo, Fabio Sciarrino

arXiv ID: 2611.12126 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Photonic processors are emerging as promising platforms in the race towards the realization of practical universal quantum computers. Several architectures with universal capabilities have been proposed for their implementation via a photonic platform, each with their own set of benefits and drawbacks. In this work we propose an architecture for a universal photonic quantum computer. The proposed architecture is modular, allowing for a high degree of flexibility and scalability, and relies on a loop-based structure, significantly reducing the number of physical components required to implement it experimentally. We prove that our architecture is universal, deterministic, and compatible with the quantum circuital model, as well as reprogrammable and capable of adaptive measurements. Furthermore, we showcase its functioning via numerical simulation on specific examples, by using machine learning techniques on a set of fundamental linear and nonlinear optical components to obtain some of the building blocks used in the architecture. The obtained results can be used to highlight the benefits and the drawbacks of the proposed architecture, as well as the route for future developments towards its physical implementation.

arXiv ID: 2611.11990 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Trapped ions is one of the promising platforms for realizing quantum information processing and quantum simulation. Selective and rapid loading of a specific isotope lays the critical foundation for such purpose particularly when scaling up the system size. Here we demonstrate a new method for rapid isotope-selective loading of 137Ba+^{137}\mathrm{Ba}^{+} or 135Ba+^{135}\mathrm{Ba}^{+}, two types of promising ion qubits, from naturally abundant source using a three-step, ultraviolet-free photoionization scheme. Neutral atoms are selected on the narrow 791 nm 6s21S0→6s6p3Po16s^2\,{}^1S_0\rightarrow6s6p\,{}^3P_1^o transition, resonantly transferred at 554 nm to 6s6d3D16s6d\,{}^3D_1, and ionized using an existing 532 nm Raman beam. A spectral-overlap analysis based on isotope and hyperfine shifts shows relayed selectivity that the second step can further suppress undesired-isotope excitation and no contaminant ion is detected during our entire experiment. item.title: [1★] AI-Driven Discovery of Entanglement Witness in Spin Hamiltonians
item.author: Jiwei Tian, Mouyang Cheng, Mingda Li
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 1 ★

Authors: Jiwei Tian, Mouyang Cheng, Mingda Li

arXiv ID: 2611.11935 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Entanglement is a crucial resource in quantum science and engineering, but detecting it in many-body states from experimentally accessible observables remains challenging. Here we introduce EntNet, an AI-driven framework to discover compact combinations of spin observables that accurately distinguish entangled from fully separable many-body mixed states in one-dimensional spin-1/21/2 chains governed by short-range Hamiltonians. We construct local-unitary-invariant representations of measurable Pauli correlators up to four-body order, sparsely select 16 candidate invariant feature channels, and learn their spatial structure using a Transformer architecture with rotary positional embeddings. Using only expectation values of these low-order observables, EntNet achieves >98%>98\% recall on certified entangled states with near-zero false-positive rates on separable states. Remarkably, it exhibits transferability across system sizes and distinct Hamiltonian families, including frustrated and disordered spin models, with minimal loss of accuracy. Beyond detection, EntNet provides physical insight into entanglement detection by revealing a selective spatial organization of pair correlations, while its finite-temperature decision boundary tracks the excitation gap of Jordan-Wigner quasiparticles. These results establish a transferable and physically interpretable framework for data-driven discovery of entanglement witnesses from local correlation functions.

item.title: [1★] Proof of the QNEC, without assumptions and under a weight
item.author: Thomas Faulkner
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 1 ★

Authors: Thomas Faulkner

arXiv ID: 2611.11920 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

We complete a proof of the quantum null energy condition (QNEC) in the mathematical framework of Half-Sided Translations and Modular Inclusions (HST/HSMI) removing an assumption that applied to previous proofs. Here we establish a theorem, which when translated to a physical setting implies that the relative entropy comparing the state of fields outside a stationary black hole with a Hartle-Hawking (HH) state is always a convex function of the horizon cut. Previous proofs only applied when a purification with finite null energy was available. We also obtain a QNEC generalization in which the HH Hilbert space is replaced with one based on a weight which is plausibly of relevance to evaporating black holes in flat space.

Thomas Faulkner

item.title: [1★] Super-resolution quantum imaging via multiphoton correlation
item.author: Yu Gu, ..., Zhuo Xu, Jianbin Liu
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 1 ★

Authors: Yu Gu, ..., Zhuo Xu, Jianbin Liu

arXiv ID: 2611.11768 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

The resolution of conventional imaging is fundamentally constrained by the diffraction limit. Here we demonstrate that this limit can be overcome using classical thermal light, through the correlation of multiphoton subsystems. By resolving the photon numbers detected in the two arms of a Hanbury Brown-Twiss interferometer, the correlation function exhibits a narrowed peak or dip whose width is tunable via the average photon number. Temporal and spatial super-resolution enhancements up to 11.8-fold and 5.1-fold, respectively, are experimentally achieved. As a proof-of-principle experiment, a double-pinhole that is completely unresolved by standard ghost imaging becomes clearly distinguishable via the correlation of two-photon versus zero-photon. The principle of this super-resolution imaging can be interpreted as a combination of classical super-resolution imaging and quantum super-resolution imaging. This work provides a versatile platform for super-resolution imaging and lithography, and opens a new avenue for exploring the boundary between classical and nonclassical phenomena.

Abstract:

We give a general proof of the Rényi QNEC formulated using the Araki-Masuda weighted LpL_p norms for all p>2p > 2. This generalizes the algebraic proof of the QNEC applicable at p=2p=2. Our approach utilizes a weighted version of a conditional LpL_p norm which extrapolates the quantum expansion/ant-quantity. We elucidate some properties of the corresponding weighted conditional entropy both for half-sided modular inclusions and for general von Neumann subalgebras with a common cyclic and separating vector. The p=2p=2 limit computes a conditional dynamical entropy originally defined in the context of black hole dynamics.

Abstract:

We prove variants of the marginal-constrained entropy accumulation theorem (MEAT) that enable finite-size security analysis of quantum key distribution with source and detector correlations. For source correlations, our results allow for the state prepared in a given round to depend on the current setting choice and a finite number of preceding choices. For detector correlations, our results require memory effects to persist for a finite number of rounds after a registered click, and all detectors to be switched off during those rounds. These results can be combined, providing, to the best of our knowledge, the first method to jointly treat correlated source and detector imperfections in quantum key distribution. Moreover, we retain all the benefits of the MEAT, such as (but not limited to) support for on-the-fly announcements and choice of adaptive tradeoff functions. The resulting key rates can be computed via a single-round optimization amenable to existing numerical methods. We demonstrate these results on qubit BB84, and exhibit competitive key rates even in the presence of correlated source and detector imperfections.

Authors: Erik Connerty, ..., Gerasimos Angelatos, Ethan N. Evans

arXiv ID: 2611.10351 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Simulating high dimensional unstructured Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) with quantum processors is a major challenge with significant potential benefit. Existing methods have been demonstrated at small qubit counts, on simplifications of realistic problems. We implement a quantum reservoir network (QRN) for forecasting high-dimensional unstructured PDEs using up to 52 qubits on IBM superconducting hardware. Our method is gradient-free and does not suffer from the challenges of variational quantum algorithms. Instead, the QRN provides a large kernel space, up to 2^52 dimensions and beyond the reach of exact classical simulation, that remains useful under current hardware noise levels. Furthermore, a partial measure-and-reset mechanism enables total circuit runtime for ~24 times the qubit coherence time, so qubit lifetimes do not limit the forecast horizon. Thus, our method enables forecasting realistic unstructured nonlinear PDEs on quantum hardware. Typical difficulties associated with predicting large scale PDEs, such as transpilation, exponential shot requirements, hardware noise, and short qubit lifetimes are mitigated through careful design considerations and a dynamic observable reconstruction method. We validate our approach using a ~34k cell unstructured 2D cylinder flow at Reynolds number 1000 and a challenging nonlinear Gray--Scott reaction--diffusion problem, demonstrating high fidelity prediction on CUDA-Q simulation and on 26 and 52-qubit superconducting quantum processors. Specifically, we show that adding QRN features to an autoencoder linear prediction pipeline reduces prediction error by 21%-43%. Finally, we demonstrate closed-loop autoregressive PDE forecasting on these problems. This work demonstrates, for the first time, quantum circuits with depth beyond qubit lifetimes achieving accurate unstructured mesh forecasting on highly nonlinear PDEs.

item.title: [1★] Experimental visual quantum state discrimination
item.author: A. Duplinskiy, M. J. Filipovich, A. I. Lvovsky
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 1 ★

Authors: A. Duplinskiy, M. J. Filipovich, A. I. Lvovsky

arXiv ID: 2611.10282 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Almost all solutions to vision tasks —\unicode{x2014} offered by nature and technology alike —\unicode{x2014} rely on capturing an image using a lens or a similar optical instrument, followed by computational analysis by neurons of a brain or a digital computer. This approach is inherently suboptimal in photon-limited and noisy conditions, where critical information is irreversibly lost at the measurement stage. We address this gap by introducing AI-driven optimization of quantum measurements on the incoming photons, learning how to extract the maximum possible information for a given computer vision task from each incoming photon. The trained measurement consists of a diffractive optical neural network (DONN) followed by a detector array. We train the DONN with a quantum information-theoretic objective that maximizes the rate at which the discrimination error decays as photons accumulate. The resulting measurement achieves exponentially lower error than both direct imaging and a DONN optimized for single-photon discrimination. We validate the advantage in a noiseless setting as well as a photon-counting experiment with an electron-multiplying CCD with the noise corresponding to 10410^4 photons per single signal photon, where the measurement also learns to mitigate the detector noise.

Abstract:

The asymmetric quantum Rabi model, a two-level system with splitting Δ\Delta and bias ϵ\epsilon coupled with strength gg to a boson mode, has level crossings when ϵ\epsilon is an integer multiple NN of the mode frequency. They are due to a hidden symmetry operator JJ, for which no general formula has been available. Here we obtain JJ in closed form for every NN. We find that JJ is given by the parity of the symmetric model times the continuant (ordered tridiagonal determinant) of NN first-order operators, which are the Hamiltonians at the intermediate biases N−1,N−3,…,1−NN-1,N-3,\dots,1-N minus a common number operator. The symmetry is thus a staircase of NN bias steps that closes on the mirror image of the model precisely at integer bias. The proof uses induction on two commutation relations. The same relations hold in the asymmetric two-photon and two-mode models, written with the generators of su(1,1)\mathfrak{su}(1,1), so that the same continuant gives their symmetry operators for every order, previously known only for the lowest ones. We also relate the closed formula for JJ to the known recursion relations for its coefficients and give their terms of lowest order in Δ\Delta explicitly.

Abstract:

Engineering large and reproducible valley splittings is essential for the scalable operation of silicon spin qubits. In Si/SiGe quantum dot devices, valley splitting arises predominantly from atomic-scale disorder and is therefore inherently random, motivating approaches that introduce a large deterministic contribution. Strain-assisted Wiggle Wells provide a route to deterministic valley splitting by combining an oscillatory Ge concentration in the Si well with shear strain; however, generating the required strain in a manner compatible with large-scale architectures remains a challenge. Here, we propose patterned stressed thin films as a scalable approach for generating shear strain in the quantum well of Si/SiGe quantum dot devices. Finite-element simulations show that compressively stressed TiN films can generate shear strains exceeding 0.1\% at the quantum well, sufficient for deterministic valley splittings of hundreds of μeV\mu \text{eV} in strain-assisted Wiggle Wells. We show that this strain can extend across multiple quantum dots and is maintained in realistic gate geometries, providing a fabrication-compatible approach for scaling deterministic valley splitting to quantum dot arrays.

Authors: Lúcio S. Fassarella

arXiv ID: 2611.12784 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

We review the basic theory of quantum channels and develop a strategy for simulating them on digital quantum computers, drawing upon the \emphChoi-Kraus operator-sum representation and Stinespring dilation to provide a unified approach for various applications. We discuss three types of applications, offering explicit examples for each: the preparation of mixed states, measurements described by positive operator-valued measures (POVMs), and the simulation of the evolution of Markovian quantum systems. We recover fundamental concepts from quantum theory, such as the purification of a mixed state and the Naimark dilation associated with a POVM. Regarding the simulation of the evolution of a Markovian quantum system, we introduce an operator, termed the residual operator, to construct, from the system's Liouvillian, a quantum channel that serves as a first-order approximation of the quantum dynamical semigroup. This allows the simulation of quantum dynamics to be performed in a manner analogous to the Euler method for ordinary differential equations, avoiding Trotterization. We prove all the theoretical results mentioned, with the exception of the fundamental Choi-Kraus theorem concerning the operator-sum representation of quantum channels, for which we provide the appropriate references. The explicit simulations discussed were implemented using the AerSimulator from IBM's Qiskit SDK, with the corresponding code available on GitHub.

Authors: Ekaterina R. Sleptsova, Alexey A. Sokolik

arXiv ID: 2611.12783 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Magnetic edge channels, arising at the edge of a two-dimensional electron gas in a magnetic field, are topologically protected and propagate unidirectionally along the edge. Their group velocities at the Fermi level, being averaged harmonically, result in drift velocity, which is related to the edge density of states, quantum capacitance, and the velocity of edge magnetoplasmons. Using semiclassical quantization of electron skipping orbits, we show that the drift velocity equals 1/2 of the electron Fermi velocity in the limit of a large number of edge channels crossing the Fermi level. This result, being universal for a hard edge and for isotropic dispersion, is checked numerically for massive electrons and for massless electrons in graphene. The drift velocity at smooth electrostatically defined edges lacks such universality. In the case of anisotropic dispersion, the semiclassical drift velocity at the hard edge reduces to a coordinate-velocity correlation along the cyclotron orbit.

Abstract:

We identify the self-energy as the environmental response to the system, which transforms covariantly under shifts of the system--environment cut. For a semi-infinite chain with asymptotically uniform parameters, this transformation admits a fixed point that defines the asymptotic boundary self-energy (BSE), whose spectral density is the Wigner semicircle. Authors: Mohamed Serry, Jun Liu

arXiv ID: 2611.12757 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Fundamental tasks in linear systems analysis and control require evaluating infinite-horizon output energies for autonomous systems and optimal value functions for controlled systems. These quantities are characterized by Lyapunov and algebraic Riccati equations, respectively. In this work, we study promise problems for their evaluation when the system matrices are sparse and represented succinctly by Boolean circuits specifying their nonzero entries, with input length polynomial in the logarithm of the system dimension. For dissipative autonomous systems with coordinate-vector initial states, we define the succinct Lyapunov value problem (SLV). Its extension to linear-quadratic optimal control is the succinct LQR value problem (SLQRV). We prove that SLV is \BQP\BQP\BQP-hard: every problem in bounded-error quantum polynomial time (\BQP\BQP\BQP) reduces to it in polynomial time. We then establish that the more general SLQRV problem admits a quantum algorithm running in time polynomial in the succinct input length. Since SLV is a special case of SLQRV, both problems are \BQP\BQP\BQP-complete. Consequently, unless bounded-error probabilistic polynomial time coincides with \BQP\BQP\BQP, no classical randomized algorithm can solve either problem on all promised instances in time polynomial in the succinct input length.

Mohamed Serry, Jun Liu

item.author: Satyaki Manna, Arindam Mitra, Sumit Mukherjee
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 0 ★

Authors: Satyaki Manna, Arindam Mitra, Sumit Mukherjee

arXiv ID: 2611.12753 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Information can be extracted from a quantum system in a sustainable manner, allowing the system to be reused for further information extraction through subsequent interactions. We investigate the possibility of consensus between two experimentally feasible methods, namely, parallel and sequential sharing, that enable multiple observers to extract information encoded in a quantum system. We show that any statistics generated by a parallel sharing strategy can be reproduced by a sequential strategy when only two observers are involved. However, when more than two observers participate in sharing quantum correlations, certain statistics achievable through parallel strategies cannot be reproduced by sequential strategies. Moreover, we demonstrate that sharing quantum advantage through a parallel strategy is impossible for a class of communication tasks involving two decoding measurements, thereby establishing an arbitrarily large gap between the sustainability of quantum advantage under sequential and parallel strategies. This naturally raises the question of whether this impossibility extends to communication tasks involving more than two decoding measurements. We show that, while parallel sharing of quantum advantage is impossible in a 3-bit random access code (RAC), it becomes possible in a 3-bit parity-oblivious RAC, where at most two observers can simultaneously obtain a quantum advantage by performing measurements on two imperfect clones of the initially prepared quantum system. Our findings have potential applications in the development of quantum communication networks and distributed quantum information processing.

Satyaki Manna, Arindam Mitra, Sumit Mukherjee

Abstract:

We study eigenstate fluctuations of the particle number in the nearest-neighbour free-fermion model on the periodic cubic lattice (Z/LZ)d(\mathbb{Z}/L\mathbb{Z})^d. For every fixed dimension, every particle number, every subvolume, and every normalized energy eigenstate, we prove a bound of order NLd−1NL^{d-1} for the particle-number variance. The corresponding eigenstate-thermalization estimate is of order Ld−1/(Nη2)L^{d-1}/(N\eta^2) for fluctuations of relative size η\eta. The proof decomposes the centered particle-number operator according to one-particle energy transfer and treats the zero- and nonzero-transfer components separately. The nonzero-transfer part is controlled by a sharp resonance bound, proved from Mann's theorem on relations among roots of unity, while the zero-transfer part is estimated by a Hilbert-Schmidt argument. These bounds are optimal in every dimension: the maximal nonzero-gap multiplicity has order Ld−1L^{d-1}, and suitable many-body eigenstates realize matching variance lower bounds and show that the concentration bound cannot be improved in estimates uniform in the tolerance parameter.

Abstract:

In the familiar twin paradox, the traveling twin ages less than the one who stays behind as a consequence of relativistic time dilation. Here, we show that quantum postselection can effectively reverse this outcome. Using an analytically solvable quantum clock model, we demonstrate that postselection of the center-of-mass motion produces an effective time advance through anomalous weak values, even though every individual motional branch undergoes ordinary time dilation. We extend this analysis to a weak gravitational field and show that an effective time advance can arise even for simple coherent states of the quantum clock motion. We further illustrate this effect using a hydrogen-like atom, revealing how it manifests itself in the atomic wavefunction. Our results demonstrate that quantum interference and postselection can produce an effective time advance beyond conventional relativistic time dilation.

Abstract:

Ergotropy is a key quantity of a quantum battery that measures the maximum extractable energy. When the extraction process is not local, a faithful transfer of ergotropy across distance is necessary. In this work, we investigate such transfer by using spin chains with weakened coupling at the boundaries as mediator. Weakening the coupling at the two boundaries of the chain gives rise to localized edge states allowing high fidelity transfer within given time duration. We found that, for long spin chains, the transferred ergotropy alternates between even and odd number of spins. We explain this parity effect by investigating the chain spectral structure. Furthermore, we consider both the nearest-neighbor and long-range interactions between spin. In both model of interactions, weakening the boundary couplings improves the maximum transferred ergotropy for long spin chain, compared with in the case of conventional uniform chain. Although the long-range interaction reduces the transferred ergotropy, the transfer time is reduced, too, in particular for longer chain. In addition to the total transferred ergotropy, we also investigate the effect of initial states of the sender spin to the transport of the coherent and incoherent components of the total ergotropy, and the average transport efficiency.

Abstract:

Authors: Chuanlong Ma, ..., Chang-Ling Zou, Luyan Sun

arXiv ID: 2611.12481 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Distributed quantum networks are important for scalable quantum processors and for potential applications in communication, distributed computation, and sensing, in which direct classical links for adaptive control are essential to harness the shared entanglement. However, controlling superconducting quantum processors from a separate refrigerator over long distances remains elusive. Here, we introduce a coherent optical link (COL) that delivers microwave waveforms and their phase references between dilution refrigerators. Combining a laser, a microwave-to-optical transducer and an optical-to-microwave photodiode, the COL transmits microwave control signals over 10~km of fiber, while optical references derived from the same laser compensate for the frequency mismatch between devices. Through the COL, we deliver a universal gate set to a transmon qubit and a cavity qubit in another refrigerator and entangle them, and achieve a Bell-state fidelity of 80.6\%. Quantum control delivered through the COL thus provides a classical backbone for modular quantum processors.

item.title: [0★] Discrete time crystals stabilized by bounded measurement noise
item.author: Pallabi Chatterjee, Tanay Nag, Ranjan Modak
item.content:encoded:
Scites: 0 ★

Authors: Pallabi Chatterjee, Tanay Nag, Ranjan Modak

arXiv ID: 2611.12400 (arxiv.org | scirate)

Abstract:

Periodically driven clean interacting systems generically heat up, which destroys discrete time-crystalline order. Here we ask whether continuous weak measurement can stabilize such order. We study a long-range interacting spin chain whose local occupation is continuously monitored. Measurements generally induce a transition from volume-law to area-law entanglement. Yet low entanglement alone is not enough: along typical quantum trajectories, the system still reaches a featureless state with no subharmonic response. In contrast, the most-probable trajectory, obtained by suppressing measurement fluctuations, shows robust period doubling. To connect these limits, we introduce a bounded-noise protocol that restricts measurement fluctuations to a finite window. Narrow windows preserve period doubling. Intermediate windows produce coexisting time-crystalline and non-time-crystalline trajectories. Over time, trajectories leave the time-crystalline group one by one, so the order is long lived but finite. Wide windows destroy the order. Our results establish bounded measurement noise, discarding the large-deviation trajectories, as a route to time-crystalline order in clean systems. They also show that the measurement-induced area-law phase is necessary, but not sufficient, for this order.

Pallabi Chatterjee, Tanay Nag, Ranjan Modak

Abstract:

Superconducting qubits operate within a well-defined temperature range, making local temperature monitoring important. Here we show that intrinsic two-level defects in Josephson-junction barriers can act as local thermometers by exploiting the shape of their population response, without requiring calibration of the readout offset or contrast. Marginalizing over these unknown parameters imposes an identifiability requirement absent from single-parameter thermometric bounds: for narrow sweeps, usable information scales as the fourth power of the sweep width. Hence, a narrow sweep becomes locally indistinguishable from a change in offset or contrast. We illustrate this principle with a strain-swept two-level defect in a Josephson junction. For a reported defect with tunneling energy Δ0/h=\SI1.3\giga\hertz\Delta_{0}/h=\SI{1.3}{\giga\hertz}, swept along one branch of its hyperbola to \SI2.69\giga\hertz (an asymmetry excursion of \SI2.36\giga\hertz, or \SI8\volt of piezo voltage), the analysis projects a single-defect fit precision of \SI0.58\percent at \SI20\milli\kelvin. The resulting response enables temperature estimation without prior calibration of the readout offset and contrast, while the same sweep overdetermines the Boltzmann form and identifies significant deviations from thermality. These results establish intrinsic junction defects as a resource for calibration-free local thermometry and highlight identifiability as a key design criterion for primary temperature sensing.
